title: The Whack-a-Mole Maintenance Model, Revisited

body_markdown:
There’s a chapter in my first book, *Memoirs of a Hack Mechanic,* where I talk about how I approach maintenance and repairs. I liken it to the kids’ arcade game Whack-a-Mole, where, when a rodent appears out of one of a bunch of holes, you try, as quickly as possible, to beat it to death with a hammer.


Okay. Maybe you’re not like me. Maybe you manage automotive projects with a Gantt chart on the laptop or have a giant whiteboard in the garage, and cue things up with the organized precision of nuclear weapon assembly (one assumes). More power to you. Me, I’m more of a squeaky wheel guy. As I’ve long said, when you own too many cars, none of them get everything they need, and the need sometimes has to make actual noise before it gets addressed. Witness the embarrassing situation a few weeks ago where the[brake pads on my wife’s Honda Fit](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/those-pesky-brake-rotor-screws/) were worn right down to the metal. (And thanks to everyone who flagged that the screws holding the rotor to the hub aren’t Phillips as I said, but JIS.)


In fairness to myself, I’m not like this with everything. I mean, I’m the guy who spent nearly a year installing[an electrically-driven A/C system](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/the-last-piece-of-and-about-the-lotus-air-conditioning/) into my 1969 Lotus Elan +2. Where the hell was the need in *that?* And the other Lotus, the ’74 Europa,[sat in the garage for six years](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/long-dead-project-comes-to-life-patience-pays-off/) while I rebuilt and reinstalled its engine and recommissioned the car. These are not the machinations of a guy who *only* plays Whack-a-Mole. Maybe, like many people, it’s just challenging for me to find a setting between “respond to emergency” and “trudge on through the big project.”


In the book chapter, I raised the idea that the Whack-a-Mole model is really a binary threshold laid on top of a continuous landscape (former math major here). That is, you can think of a car’s needs as a surface with some degree of roughness. When the car is new, everything presumably works; it has no needs, the surface is smooth, and no moles poke their head out. As the car ages, problems develop and needs make themselves known, but you probably get used to a certain background level of roughness. Small thunks, clunks, rattles, and creaks become part of the landscape, but a larger issue like a loud exhaust will poke its head up. Then, when the car goes out of warranty, and you learn that fixing a broken window regulator will cost you $1500, you decide to live with it. Move all the way to a vintage car with its attendant grinches and groans, wind noise, maybe hard-starting and hot-running, and the car has to practically be dead in traffic for you to see that you’ve got a mole to whack.


I guess it’s natural that many of us deal with problems this way. Last week I wrote about repairing the horn in my ratty salvage-titled BMW E30 (the FrankenThirty). I jumped on it instantly to get the car through inspection, but other than that, I hadn’t worked on the car in months even though it’s been at the house since mid-summer. I realized something as a result: When the car’s major issues are that it has the wrong engine in it and the wrong nose on it from when it was rebuilt from its salvage event 24 years ago, and when, in order to address with the remaining mouse smell, both the headliner and the heater box need to come out, is it any wonder that I don’t pick fights with giant moles hanging out in plain sight on street corners drinking Mad Dog 20-20 and smoking cigarettes and saying *YOU WANT A PIECE OF ME, HACK BOY* , and instead just drive it and wait for moles that are small enough to whack?


I realized that there’s another dynamic, which is that, when you buy a car, even if it’s well-used, it’s new to *you* , so you have fresh eyes and see moles to whack everywhere, but you may be myopic and not seeing the car’s actual needs. I thought back to when I bought the FrankenThirty, but before I knew that it was a mouse-riddled Franken-car. From the ad on Facebook Marketplace, I could see that the driver’s-side Recaro-style sport seat was badly worn, so even before I drove out to look at the car, I began looking for a replacement seat, or at least the piece to replace the worn bolster.


The driver-swapped-to-passenger seat. In addition to the ripped bolster, the bottom piece is lumpy and uncomfortable. Good thing I don’t have to sit in it.


Rob Siegel


After I picked up the car, I spent hours trying to find a well-priced, fully functional Blaupunkt CM5908 “pyramid” radio, as the one in the car appears to be fried.


It’s the original Blaupunkt; it powers on, it accepts the code, but it’s cooked inside.


Rob Siegel


Of course, when I realized the extent of the car’s salvage issues, I pined wistfully for those innocent times just two days earlier when I was obsessing over seats and stereos. In one of those “for now” moves that become permanent, I swapped driver and passenger seats, laid an old satellite-and-subwoofer sound system on the floor and back deck, and have barely thought about these two moles since.


I did something similar with the Armada. Shortly after I bought it, one of my kids borrowed it, ran the battery down overnight, and for some reason, the key fob (which you use not just to lock and unlock the car but whose proximity also lets you twist the ignition without inserting the key) quit working. Unlocking, starting, and locking the truck with the tiny key that’s meant to stay inside the fob is awkward. I spent a lot of time trying to get it working, poring over posts in the Armada forums, trying to reprogram it and the second fob the truck came with, and never got it to work. Then I got overwhelmed by the car’s myriad exhaust, suspension, air conditioning, and actuator issues, and hadn’t thought about the key fob until now.


I’ve gotten used to using this never-really-meant-to-be-taken-out-of-the-key-fob key.


Rob Siegel


As I’ve described, living with the ’69 Lotus Elan +2 has been both exhilarating and frustrating. The car is a bit of a tease, making me think it’s sorted enough to jump in and drive anywhere, only to suddenly present a mole that requires immediate and total obliteration. The most recent one appeared when I was about to take the car on a drive on a crisp, clear fall day, and found that the temperature and fuel gauges weren’t working. The gas gauge is a minor issue, but not knowing if this engine with its expensive bespoke Lotus Twin-Cam head is running hot is a no-go condition for me. Fortunately, it turned out to be a connector that had popped off the voltage stabilizer that feeds both gauges. Unfortunately, it was way up under the dash, so I guess you could say I had to chase the mole into its hole, Bill Murray-in-Caddyshack-style.


So there you go. May your surfaces of automotive needs be acceptably smooth (or, as my urologist would say, “smooth and unremarkable”), and if they’re not, may you flatten those little suckers with all deliberate haste.


***
